newsitem.title: EGYPT: Deregulation advocate promoted in Egyptian cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Deregulation advocate promoted in Egyptian cabinet.

text.p: Egyptian Prime Minister Kamal Ganzouri shuffled his cabinet for the first time in 18 months on Tuesday, promoting a young and dynamic advocate of deregulation and rapid privatisation to the Ministry of Economy.
Youssef Boutros-Ghali, 44-year-old nephew of the former U.N. secretary-general, took the oath of office as economy minister in front of President Hosni Mubarak in a televised ceremony.
The appointment was one of nine changes announced so far, most of them in the lower echelons of the cabinet.

Cabinet members with the key portfolios -- Defence Minister Field Marshal Mohamed Hussein Tantawi, Foreign Minister Amr Moussa and Interior Minister Hassan el-Alfi -- will remain in their jobs, sources close to the government said.

Boutros-Ghali, a U.S.-educated academic said to be impatient with the pace of economic liberalisation, has been a junior economic minister in Ganzouri's office since the prime minister took office in January 1996.
An articulate and confident public speaker, he has played a leading role in promoting Egypt to foreign investors and in talks with institutions such as the International Monetary Fund.
He replaces Nawal el-Tatawi, a former banker who was one of the first Egyptian women to rise to such high cabinet rank.

"He is probably the best sort of person for the job because he has the best track record. He is highly reform- minded and he really is a reformer by deep conviction and training," said an international economic analyst based in Cairo.

Boutros-Ghali, in a recent interview with Reuters, said one of the government's aims was to dismantle what he called "the predatory state", a reference to the old centrally planned economic system which preyed on private enterprise.
He is said to favour privatisation of one of the major utilities, such as the telecommunications authority -- a step that Ganzouri's government has not yet dared to take.
The new economy minister is also the first Coptic Christian to join the cabinet since his uncle Boutros Boutros-Ghali was deputy prime minister for a brief period in the early 1990s.

But it is not yet clear to what extent Boutros-Ghali will be able to direct economic policy, which is dominated by Ganzouri, Finance Minister Mohieddin el-Gharib and Public Enterprise Minister Atef Obeid, who runs the privatisation programme.
The business community says Tatawi made little impact, partly because the economy ministry has a limited mandate.
In other changes, Ganzouri appointed Mahmoud Abu Zaid to the Ministry of Public Works and Water Resources. The post had been vacant since Abdel-Hadi Radi died in November.
He removed some of the many peripheral responsibilities of Atef Obeid, who was also in charge of environmental affairs and civil service reform.
Nadia Makram Obeid, a woman from a prominent Coptic family with a long history in Egyptian politics, took the oath of office as Minister of Environmental Affairs, a new post.
Mohamed Zaki Abu Amer, formerly a minister of state for parliamentary affairs, becomes minister of state for administrative development, or civil service reform.

Another woman, former Egyptian ambassador to Japan Mervat el-Tellawi, is now minister of social affairs and social insurance. She replaces Amal Osman, who had held the post since the 1970s under late President Anwar Sadat.
The other survivor from the Sadat era, Electricity Minister Maher Abaza, has not been tipped for replacement.

Ganzouri has also reorganised the Education Ministry, appointing Moufid Shehab as minister of higher education and minister of state for scientific research. Shehab has been chancellor of Cairo University.
Education Minister Hussein Kamel Bahaeddin retains his post but is no longer in charge of higher education.
